flags.line: It can weaken the acute subjective effects of psychedelics. FRANK says mixing drugs is always risky.
flags.why: 'It' names nothing; the review covers antidepressants only, not the other psychiatric medicines asked about; and 'is the mix risky?' gets FRANK's line on all mixing, while the review's finding on this mix, listed under the short, goes unsaid.
flags.say: Name what weakens what (antidepressants can weaken how strongly a psychedelic trip is felt), say the review covers antidepressants only, and give what it says of the risk of this mix, with its own hedges, beside FRANK's general warning.

flags.line: It can weaken the acute subjective effects of psychedelics. FRANK says mixing drugs is always risky.
flags.why: 'Acute subjective effects' leads the answer to an everyday question where plain words exist (how strong the trip feels); the But's 'dose-response relationships' and 'classic psychedelics' are lab words too.
flags.say: Write how strongly the trip is felt, not acute subjective effects, and say the But in everyday words (how the doses of the two drugs work together is not well understood).

flags.line: Adults (18 years and over); Recommended maximum caffeine daily intake.
flags.why: The earlier version was held for leaving out a group the body excepts (pregnant women). Health Canada's table, as I recall it, also gives a lower amount for pregnancy and breastfeeding; this quote cannot show it, so please check.
flags.say: Give every group the body names among adults, each with its own amount in its own words, so that a row for adults is not read as covering pregnant or breastfeeding women.

flags.line: Kava is a popular medicinal herb. Its most concerning risk is liver injury, and there is compelling evidence it is linked to some toxicities.
flags.why: Asked what kava is like, it says only that kava is a popular medicinal herb, nothing of what it does to people or how it feels; only the 'Not complete yet' label hints at the gap.
flags.say: Answer what kava is like only from a source that says what it does to people; until one is read, lead with its risks and say the answer is about its risks.

flags.line: The review says kava hepatotoxicity was the most concerning adverse effect of consumption.
flags.why: 'Hepatotoxicity' and 'adverse effect' are clinical words where plain ones exist (liver damage, harm); the short's 'toxicities' is the same.
flags.say: Write liver damage, not hepatotoxicity, and harm, not adverse effect or toxicities.

flags.line: Yes. The brain becomes less sensitive to caffeine, so higher doses are needed for the same effect. Performance benefits also decrease over time.
flags.why: 'Performance benefits also decrease over time' comes from one study of 11 healthy, active adults whose results 'suggest' tolerance to caffeine's help with exercise; the line drops the hedge and widens it to anyone's performance.
flags.say: Say whose performance and which: one small study of 11 healthy, active adults suggests caffeine's boost to exercise shrank over 20 days.

flags.line: That study found caffeine still helped performance after 20 days, but the effect was smaller than at the start.
flags.why: 'That study' points to no line the reader sees (the one naming it is gone), so it reads as the 2025 review of older adults; it was 11 healthy, active adults tested on exercise, and its quote says 'suggests'.
flags.say: Name the study in the line itself, with whom it tested and what it measured (a 2019 study of 11 healthy, active adults, on exercise), and keep its 'suggests'.

flags.line: It can be found in urine, but few tests check for it. Tianeptine leaves the body quickly, with a half-life of 2.5 hours.
flags.why: Asked how long tianeptine stays and can be found, it gives a half-life, unexplained; a half-life (the time for half of it to leave the blood) is not how long a test can find it, as the editor has held.
flags.say: Give how long a test can find tianeptine only where a source says so; where a half-life is kept, explain it plainly and do not offer it as how long the drug stays.

flags.line: No. A review says trying to cut supply via law enforcement is less effective than hoped. In Georgia, massive street drug testing did not reduce drug use.
flags.why: The flat 'No' says more than its quotes: one review calls cutting supply through law enforcement 'less effective than hoped', not ineffective, and the other is one country's case study of street drug testing.
flags.say: Answer in the sources' own measure: a review says law enforcement aimed at supply has been costly and less effective than hoped, and in Georgia mass street drug testing brought no measurable fall in use.

flags.line: No. A review says trying to cut supply via law enforcement is less effective than hoped. In Georgia, massive street drug testing did not reduce drug use.
flags.why: The question asks whether crackdowns cut use or just move it elsewhere; 'No' to an either-or question is unclear, and nothing in the short says whether use moves elsewhere.
flags.say: Say which half of the question the answer covers, and answer whether crackdowns move drug use elsewhere only from a source that speaks of that.

flags.line: The review also says criminalization has prompted people who use drugs to adopt more dangerous practices in riskier settings.
flags.why: The quote stands in the review's country example on Nigeria and begins 'It has also prompted'; the line names criminalization in general as the cause, and does not say Nigeria.
flags.say: Say where it was seen, in the review's own terms (its example of Nigeria), name the cause only as the review does, and write 'making drug use a crime', not criminalization.

flags.line: It can be found in urine for 24-48 hours, blood for 12-24 hours, or hair for up to 90 days. It is not on standard drug tests.
flags.why: The page says 'not commonly tested for on standard panel drug tests'; 'It is not on standard drug tests' is surer, and the urine time is for specialist testing, which the short drops.
flags.say: Keep the page's own strength and scope: standard drug tests do not commonly look for etomidate, and the 24-48 hours in urine is for specialist testing.

flags.line: A 2021 review reports an elimination half-life of 2.9–5.5 h in ASA class I/II patients.
flags.why: 'Elimination half-life' and 'ASA class I/II patients' are hospital words a reader who left school early would not follow; they mean half of it leaves the blood in about 3 to 5.5 hours, in fairly healthy people having anaesthesia.
flags.say: Say it plainly: in fairly healthy people given etomidate in hospital, half of it leaves the blood in about 3 to 5.5 hours, which is not how long a test can find it.
